areas.name: Left console
areas.text: The left console beside the pilot holds the engine start, electrical power, fuel, radio, lights and flight control test panels, and the canopy controls. The throttle lever sits above it.

panels.name: ENG & JET START control panel
panels.text: This panel starts the engine. It has the switch for the jet fuel starter (JFS), a small helper engine that spins the big engine until it can run by itself.
panels.context: The start-up order is: main power to BATT, JFS switch to START, then the throttle to idle when the engine has enough speed.

controls.name: JFS RUN light
controls.text: This light comes on within 30 seconds after the jet fuel starter was switched on. It shows that the helper engine runs at its right speed.
controls.context: The pilot waits for it before going on with the engine start.

controls.name: JFS switch (jet fuel starter)

positions.name: START 1
positions.text: Uses one of the two pressure bottles (accumulators). In BMS this starts the helper engine only about every second time; after a failed try the other bottle is still full.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The jet fuel starter is off. During a normal ground start it turns itself off at about half engine speed and the switch snaps back to OFF.

positions.name: START 2
positions.text: Uses both pressure bottles at once, which gives a much better chance to start. This is the choice in cold weather.

controls.text: This switch starts a small helper engine, the jet fuel starter (JFS). The helper engine spins the big jet engine until the big engine can run on its own. It works like a car's starter motor, only much stronger.
controls.context: It is the main step of the engine start, after MAIN PWR is set. A green RUN light shows the starter runs; at about a quarter of engine speed the pilot moves the throttle to idle. START 2 gives the better chance, especially in cold weather.

controls.name: ENG CONT switch (engine control)

positions.name: PRI
positions.text: Primary mode, the normal mode. The digital electronic control manages the engine and afterburner. The guard is kept down.

positions.name: SEC
positions.text: Secondary mode. No afterburner, the nozzle stays closed and engine limits are off.

controls.text: This switch picks which computer controls the engine. PRI is the normal electronic control. SEC is the older backup control that uses only the mechanical fuel system.
controls.context: In SEC the afterburner is not available. The SEC caution light on the caution panel comes on.

controls.name: AB RESET switch

positions.name: AB RESET
positions.text: Resets the engine computer; the switch springs back to NORM.

positions.name: ENG DATA
positions.text: Records a few seconds of engine data; the switch springs back to NORM.

controls.text: A spring-loaded switch that returns to NORM. AB RESET resets the engine's control computer (DEEC) and can clear an engine fault. ENG DATA records engine data for the ground crew.
controls.context: The engine failure checklists of the manual use AB RESET, then NORM, as one of the first steps.

controls.name: MAX POWER switch

positions.name: MAX POWER
positions.text: The manual does not describe this position.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The manual does not describe this position.

controls.text: A switch of the engine control. The BMS manual lists it for the PW220 engine only as an electrical consumer; it does not describe what it does.
controls.context: The switch is on the ENG & JET START panel next to the AB RESET switch.

panels.name: EPU control panel (emergency power)
panels.text: The emergency power unit (EPU) is a small backup motor that gives hydraulic and electric power for about 10 to 15 minutes if the engine fails. This panel controls it.
panels.context: The EPU normally stays on automatic. It starts by itself when both generators fail or both hydraulic systems lose pressure. On the ground the EPU safety pin keeps it off; in BMS the ground crew removes it through the ATC menu.

controls.name: EPU switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Commands the EPU off. In flight it stays off unless both generators fail.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Automatic. The EPU starts by itself if the generators are lost or both hydraulic systems fail.

controls.text: This switch sets the emergency power unit to automatic or switches it by hand.
controls.context: NORM is the normal position in flight.

controls.name: EPU run light
controls.text: This light is on when the EPU runs and its hydraulic pump gives more than 2000 psi.
controls.context: It tells the pilot that the emergency power really works.

controls.name: AIR light
controls.text: This light is on whenever the EPU has been told to run and its safety pin is removed. It stays on even when the EPU also burns hydrazine.
controls.context: The EPU can use engine air or its special fuel.

controls.name: HYDRAZN light
controls.text: This light is on when the EPU is told to burn its special fuel, hydrazine, whether any is left or not.
controls.context: Hydrazine is needed when the engine is slow or has failed.

panels.name: ELEC control panel (electrical power)
panels.text: This panel controls the plane's electricity: where it comes from and whether it is working. Its lights tell what has failed.
panels.context: The pilot uses it first when getting into the cockpit and again to reset a generator after a caution.

controls.name: MAIN PWR switch

positions.name: MAIN PWR
positions.text: The engine's generator, or a ground power cart, powers the aircraft. The standby generator is enabled.

positions.name: BATT
positions.text: Only the battery gives power, to the battery bus. This is enough for the first checks.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No electricity from the generator. The cockpit is dark.

controls.text: This is the main power switch of the whole plane. It decides where electricity comes from: nowhere, the battery, or the engine's generator.
controls.context: It is the first switch the pilot moves when climbing into the cockpit. The engine must be started with the switch at MAIN PWR: a start on battery power can lead to a hot or hung start and leaves systems dead.

controls.name: ELEC CAUTION RESET button
controls.text: Pressing this button clears the electrical caution lights and resets the two generators.
controls.context: The pilot presses it after a generator trips.

controls.name: FLCS PMG light
controls.text: This light is on when the flight control computers do not get power from their own small generator.
controls.context: It is a fault light for the flight controls.

controls.name: MAIN GEN light
controls.text: This light is on when no power comes from the main generator or from outside.
controls.context: It is normal on the ground before the engine runs.

controls.name: STBY GEN light
controls.text: This light is on when the standby generator gives no power.
controls.context: The standby generator is the backup to the main one.

controls.name: EPU GEN light
controls.text: This light is on when the emergency unit was told to start but gives no power to the emergency buses.
controls.context: A bus is a group of electric lines.

controls.name: EPU PMG light
controls.text: This light is on when the EPU generator does not feed all parts of the flight control system.
controls.context: It matters only when the EPU runs.

controls.name: ACFT BATT FAIL light
controls.text: This light is on when the battery has failed (20 volts or less).
controls.context: It is a battery problem warning.

controls.name: ACFT BATT TO FLCS light
controls.text: This light is on when the flight control computers run on battery power.
controls.context: It shows that the flight controls lost their normal power.

panels.name: Fuel control panel
panels.text: This panel has the fuel master valve, the fuel pump selector and the switches for the tank pressure and the refuelling door.
panels.context: Most of the time the pilot leaves it as set. It matters in a fuel imbalance or an emergency.

controls.name: FUEL MASTER switch
controls.text: This switch opens or closes the main fuel valve to the engine. It normally stays at MASTER with the guard down.
controls.context: Closing it stops fuel to the engine.

controls.name: TANK INERTING switch

positions.name: TANK INERTING
positions.text: Would fill the tanks with halon; not implemented in BMS.

controls.text: This switch would pump a special gas (halon) into the fuel tanks to lower the risk of fire. The BMS training manual says the TANK INERTING switch is not implemented.
controls.context: In the real aircraft it is only for combat or emergencies, for example after battle damage.

controls.name: ENGINE FEED knob

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Both pumps off. A different system feeds the engine.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Both pumps on. The fuel balance is kept automatically.

positions.name: AFT
positions.text: Only the aft tank pump runs, which moves fuel forward.

positions.name: FWD
positions.text: Only the forward tank pump runs, which moves fuel backward.

controls.text: This knob switches the fuel pumps and can move the plane's balance point by choosing which tank group feeds the engine.
controls.context: The pilot sets it to NORM before flight, because with the pumps off the fuel system can fail later in the flight. AFT and FWD are used when the fuel gauge needles show an imbalance.

controls.name: AIR REFUEL switch

positions.name: OPEN
positions.text: The refuelling door opens and the tank pressure goes down.

positions.name: CLOSE
positions.text: The door closes and the tanks are pressurised again.

controls.text: This switch opens the refuelling door on the top of the plane, so it can take fuel from a tanker in the air. It also turns on the refuelling lights.
controls.context: Below 400 knots, opening it sets the flight controls to the take-off and landing settings.

panels.name: Canopy, manual pitch override and defog controls
panels.text: Controls on the left rail of the cockpit: the canopy switch and handle, the canopy emergency jettison handle, the defog lever and the manual pitch override switch.
panels.context: The canopy is the clear glass roof. The pilot closes and locks it before flight.

controls.name: MANUAL PITCH override switch

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Normal operation. The switch springs back to it.

positions.name: OVRD
positions.text: More tail power. Stick roll and yaw commands are blocked while it is held.

controls.text: Held to OVRD, this switch gives the tail surfaces more power to push the nose down in a deep stall. A deep stall is a spin-like fall where the plane does not respond.
controls.context: It is for an emergency and springs back to NORM when released.

controls.name: Canopy switch

positions.name: UP
positions.text: Raises the canopy to full open. The switch springs back to the middle.

positions.name: DOWN
positions.text: Lowers the canopy. It must be held there.

controls.text: This switch opens and closes the canopy with a motor. It must be held to move the canopy and springs back to the middle.
controls.context: The canopy handle must be in the unlocked position first. The canopy can be stopped at any time by letting the switch go.

controls.name: Canopy handle

positions.name: UNLOCKED
positions.text: The seal is let out and the canopy can move.

positions.name: LOCKED
positions.text: The canopy is locked and sealed.

controls.text: This handle (the pilots call it the yellow spider) locks the canopy and fills the seal around it with air. Moving it also switches the CANOPY warning light.
controls.context: With the canopy closed and the handle locked, the ECS starts and the CANOPY warning light goes out. This must be done before the jet fuel starter is switched on.

controls.name: CANOPY JETTISON T-handle
controls.text: Pulling this T-shaped handle throws the canopy off the plane in an emergency.
controls.context: It is a backup if the canopy does not come off when the ejection handle is pulled.

controls.name: DEFOG lever

positions.name: MIN
positions.text: Most air goes to the vents behind the seat.

positions.name: MAX
positions.text: Most air goes to the front canopy and the vent at the instrument panel.

controls.text: This lever should send more warm air to the canopy to clear fog on the glass. The BMS manual says the defog lever and cockpit heat are not implemented yet.
controls.context: MIN and MAX are the two ends of the lever.

panels.name: AUDIO 1 control panel
panels.text: This panel sets the volume of the two radios and of several warning sounds, and the squelch and guard modes of the radios.
panels.context: COMM 1 is the UHF radio and COMM 2 is the VHF radio. UHF and VHF are radios for talking to other aircraft and the tower.

controls.name: COMM 1 power/volume knob (UHF)
controls.text: Turning this knob up makes the UHF radio louder. Turned fully left, it switches the radio off.
controls.context: The pilot sets it before talking.

controls.name: COMM 1 mode knob (UHF)

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Squelch off. The manual says this is not implemented.

positions.name: SQL
positions.text: Squelch is on, the normal position.

positions.name: GD
positions.text: The radio is tuned to the guard frequency 243.0 MHz.

controls.text: This knob chooses between OFF, SQL (squelch) and GD (guard) for the UHF radio. Squelch cuts the hiss when nobody talks. Guard tunes the radio to the emergency frequency.
controls.context: GD does not work while the C & I knob is at BACK UP; then guard is chosen on the UHF backup panel. The manual says squelch OFF and pushing the knob are not implemented.

controls.name: COMM 2 power/volume knob (VHF)
controls.text: Turning this knob up makes the VHF radio louder. Turned fully left, it switches the radio off.
controls.context: The pilot sets it before talking.

controls.name: COMM 2 mode knob (VHF)

positions.name: SQL
positions.text: Squelch is on, the normal position.

positions.name: GD
positions.text: The radio is tuned to the guard frequency 121.5 MHz.

controls.text: This knob chooses between OFF, SQL (squelch) and GD (guard) for the VHF radio. Squelch cuts the hiss when nobody talks. Guard tunes the radio to the emergency frequency.
controls.context: The manual says the squelch function of this knob is not implemented yet.

controls.name: SECURE VOICE knob
controls.text: A volume knob for the coded radio. The BMS manual says the secure voice knob is not implemented.
controls.context: Coded radio is not used in BMS.

controls.name: MSL tone knob
controls.text: Turning this knob up makes the sound of the AIM-9 missile seeker louder.
controls.context: The seeker tone tells the pilot that the missile sees a target. The knob has no OFF position, so the pilot checks it during the start-up.

controls.name: TF tone knob
controls.text: A volume knob for the terrain-following system. The BMS manual says the TF knob is not implemented.
controls.context: The terrain-following radar has no tone knob that works in BMS.

controls.name: THREAT tone knob
controls.text: Turning this knob up makes the sounds of the radar warning receiver louder.
controls.context: The tones tell about new radars and missile launches. The knob has no OFF position, so the pilot checks it during the start-up.

panels.name: AUDIO 2 control panel
panels.text: This panel sets the volume of the intercom, the TACAN and the ILS, and has a mode switch for the radios.
panels.context: The TACAN and ILS are radio aids for navigation. Their volume lets the pilot hear the Morse code that names the station.

controls.name: INTERCOM knob
controls.text: Turning this knob up makes everything the pilot hears in the headset louder: the radios, the warning tones and the voice messages.
controls.context: The training manual sets it to full right and fine-tunes the single volumes on the other knobs.

controls.name: TACAN knob
controls.text: This knob would set the volume of the TACAN station name in Morse code. The BMS manual says the TACAN volume is not implemented; the knob is always treated as on.
controls.context: The TACAN is a ground beacon that gives direction and distance.

controls.name: ILS power/volume knob
controls.text: Turning this knob up switches the ILS receiver on and sets the volume of the marker sound. Turned fully left to OFF, the ILS is off.
controls.context: The ILS gives radio beams that lead the plane down to a runway. The pilot must power it to see the ILS marks.

controls.name: HOT MIC CIPHER switch

positions.name: HOT MIC
positions.text: Direct talking to the ground crew or boom operator.

positions.name: CIPHER
positions.text: Only coded radio signals are let through.

controls.text: This switch sets the mode of the intercom and radios. The BMS manual says the HOT MIC switch is not implemented.
controls.context: In the real aircraft HOT MIC is for talking to the tanker's boom operator.

panels.name: IFF control panel
panels.text: A backup panel for the IFF transponder, the radio box that answers who-are-you questions from radars with a code. It also chooses whether the radios are set from the keypad or from backup panels.
panels.context: In normal flight the keypad (ICP) does this. This panel is used if the keypad fails or by choice.

controls.name: MASTER knob (IFF power and mode)

positions.name: STBY
positions.text: Powered but unable to answer questions.

positions.name: LOW
positions.text: Works normally, but answers only from half the distance.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Normal operation: it asks and answers.

positions.name: EMER
positions.text: It answers with a fixed emergency code.

controls.text: This knob switches the IFF system on and sets how it works. It must be lifted to move to or from OFF and to EMER.
controls.context: It works whatever the C & I knob is set to.

controls.name: M-4 CODE switch (mode 4 secret code)

positions.name: A/B
positions.text: Normal: the plane uses the secret code of bank A or B.

positions.name: HOLD
positions.text: Switched to for a moment, it saves the codes when the IFF is turned off.

controls.text: This switch handles the secret code of Mode 4. ZERO erases both codes when held for two seconds. HOLD keeps them when the IFF is turned off.
controls.context: A/B is the normal position; the switch springs back to it from HOLD, and is locked in ZERO.

controls.name: C & I knob (comms and IFF control)

positions.name: UFC
positions.text: The keypad controls the IFF and the UHF radio.

positions.name: BACK UP
positions.text: The IFF panel and the UHF backup panel control them.

controls.text: This knob chooses whether the IFF and the UHF radio are controlled from the keypad (UFC) or from the backup panels.
controls.context: BACK UP is used on the ramp before the keypad has power, or if the keypad fails. The training manual starts in BACK UP and turns to UFC after the engine start.

controls.name: IFF ENABLE switch

positions.name: M3/MS
positions.text: Modes 3 and S are on; the manual says Mode S is not implemented.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Modes 1, 3 and S are off in backup.

controls.text: This switch picks which IFF code modes are on when the backup panel is used. It matters only with C & I at BACK UP.
controls.context: The normal IFF settings are made on the IFF pages of the keypad display.

controls.name: MODE 1 and MODE 3 code selectors
controls.text: Small thumb-operated selectors with number windows for the Mode 1 and Mode 3 IFF codes. They are used only with C & I at BACK UP. The Mode 3 code always ends in 00.
controls.context: For example, windows set to 77 give the Mode 3 code 7700.

controls.name: IFF MODE 4 REPLY switch
controls.text: This switch chooses which secret code answers Mode 4 questions in backup. OUT stops all replies to Mode 4 questions.
controls.context: It is used with C & I at BACK UP. With C & I at UFC the code is chosen on the keypad.

controls.name: IFF MODE 4 MONITOR switch

positions.name: AUDIO
positions.text: The tone is played on the intercom.

controls.text: This switch lets the pilot hear a tone from the IFF system. The tone tells that the system could not answer a Mode 4 question correctly.
controls.context: It only adds a tone; it changes nothing else. It is used with C & I at BACK UP.

panels.name: UHF backup control panel
panels.text: This panel is a backup control for the UHF radio (the ARC-164). It has a frequency display, preset channels and knobs to tune a frequency by hand.
panels.context: It works on battery power, so it is the only radio usable before the engine runs. It is the radio control when C & I is at BACK UP.

controls.name: CHAN knob (preset channel)
controls.text: Turning this knob picks a preset channel, a stored frequency, like a station button on a car radio. 19 channels are available.
controls.context: It works when the mode knob is at PRESET. By default the panel starts on channel 6.

controls.name: Manual frequency knobs
controls.text: Five knobs that set one digit each of the radio frequency, from the 100 MHz digit down to the 0.025 MHz digit.
controls.context: They work when the mode knob is at MNL. The frequency may be from 225.000 to 399.975 MHz.

controls.name: Function knob

positions.name: MAIN
positions.text: The radio works on the chosen frequency.

positions.name: BOTH
positions.text: The radio works and also listens to the guard frequency 243.0 MHz.

controls.text: This knob powers the backup radio panel and picks the receiver mode.
controls.context: With the C & I knob at BACK UP, OFF also cuts power to the UHF radio. The COMM 1 knob on the AUDIO 1 panel must not be at OFF either.

controls.name: Mode knob

positions.name: MNL
positions.text: The radio uses the frequency set with the manual knobs.

positions.name: PRESET
positions.text: The radio uses the preset channel.

positions.name: GRD
positions.text: The radio is set to 243.0 MHz.

controls.text: This knob chooses how the radio is tuned: by hand, by preset or to the guard frequency.
controls.context: GRD is the emergency frequency 243.0 MHz.

controls.name: TONE button
controls.text: Pressing this button sends a tone on the radio frequency. The BMS manuals do not describe it.
controls.context: It sends the tone on the tuned frequency.

controls.name: SQUELCH switch
controls.text: This switch turns the squelch on or off. Squelch cuts the hiss when nobody talks.
controls.context: With squelch on the radio is quiet until a signal comes.

controls.name: VOL knob
controls.text: A small volume knob. The BMS manual says the knob is not meant to work; in BMS it balances the voices of the computer-flown aircraft against the voices of human pilots.
controls.context: The main UHF volume is set with the COMM 1 knob on the AUDIO 1 panel.

controls.name: TEST DISPLAY button
controls.text: Pressing this button lights every part of the display windows to test them.
controls.context: It is a quick check that the display works.

controls.name: STATUS button
controls.text: While pressed, this button shows the frequency the radio is tuned to in the display.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to check what frequency a preset channel has.

panels.name: EXT LIGHTING control panel
panels.text: This panel controls the lights on the outside of the plane: position lights, the flashing anti-collision light, formation lights, and the refuelling lights.
panels.context: Outside lights help others see the plane at night and in formation. A master knob can overrule the other switches.

controls.name: POSITION FLASH/STEADY switch
controls.text: This switch makes the position lights flash or glow steadily.
controls.context: Position lights are the red and green lights at the wingtips and the white one at the tail.

controls.name: POSITION WING/TAIL switch
controls.text: This switch sets the position lights on the wingtips, the intake and the tail to bright or dim.
controls.context: At OFF the wingtip lights follow the FORM knob instead.

controls.name: FUSELAGE switch
controls.text: This switch controls the lights on the fuselage that light up the tall tail.
controls.context: They help others see the plane at night.

controls.name: ANTI-COLL knob (anti-collision light)
controls.text: This knob sets the flash pattern of the anti-collision light, a bright flashing light that warns other aircraft. OFF switches it off. The other positions give seven flash patterns.
controls.context: The patterns are 1 to 4 and A, B and C. The training manual uses patterns 1 to 4 on the ramp and at the line-up, and turns the light off while taxiing.

controls.name: FORM knob (formation lights)
controls.text: Turning this knob changes the brightness of the formation lights, the strip lights on the wingtips and the fuselage.
controls.context: They help pilots flying close together at night.

controls.name: AERIAL REFUELING knob
controls.text: Turning this knob changes the brightness of the lights that light the refuelling receptacle on top of the plane.
controls.context: It works only when the AIR REFUEL switch is at OPEN.

controls.name: MASTER knob (exterior lights)
controls.text: This knob is the master for the exterior lights and overrules the other switches. At NORM the individual switches and knobs work as set. In the COVERT positions the strobe is off and an invisible infrared light is on for pilots with night vision goggles.
controls.context: The manual names COVERT ALL and COVERT A-C for the strobe light. The other positions limit which lights may be on.

panels.name: FLT CONTROL panel
panels.text: This panel has manual settings for the flight control system, the computers between the stick and the control surfaces. It is normally not used because the system works by itself.
panels.context: The pilot uses it for the flight control self-test during start-up and in case of failures.

controls.name: DIGITAL BACKUP switch
controls.text: This switch tells the flight control computers to use their backup software. The DBU ON warning light comes on and the HUD shows a flashing WARN.
controls.context: It is for a failure of the main software. The training manual has the pilot test it once during the start-up and put the switch back to OFF afterwards.

controls.name: MANUAL TF FLY-UP switch

positions.name: ENABLE
positions.text: Fly-ups are allowed also in manual terrain following.

controls.text: This switch belongs to the terrain-following radar. With ENABLE, the plane makes an automatic fly-up when the terrain-following radar warns of an obstacle, also in manual terrain following. It must be down for the flight control self-test.
controls.context: The training manual warns that the FLCS BIT is likely to fail if this switch is up.

controls.name: ALT FLAPS switch

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Flaps are set by the flight control computers.

positions.name: EXTEND
positions.text: The flaps are lowered by hand.

controls.text: This switch lowers the rear flaps of the wings by hand. Flaps give more lift at low speed.
controls.context: It is used if they did not lower with the landing gear.

controls.name: FLCS RUN / FAIL lights
controls.text: A green light and a red light. Green RUN is on while the self-test runs. Red FAIL is on if the test finds a problem.
controls.context: A failure is also shown on the fault list display.

controls.name: LE FLAPS switch

positions.name: AUTO
positions.text: The front flaps are set automatically.

positions.name: LOCK
positions.text: The front flaps are locked and the FLCS warning light comes on.

controls.text: This switch locks the front flaps of the wings (leading edge flaps) in place. AUTO is the normal position. When they are locked, the FLCS warning light comes on.
controls.context: It could be used if a front flap fails and the flaps are uneven.

controls.name: FLCS RESET switch
controls.text: This switch resets the flight control warning lights and some faults, if their cause is gone.
controls.context: It is used after a fault has cleared.

controls.name: FLCS BIT switch
controls.text: This switch starts the self-test of the flight controls on the ground. The test takes about 45 seconds and moves the control surfaces.
controls.context: It is done during start-up and works only on the ground at low speed. All other switches of this panel must be down, or the test is likely to fail.

panels.name: MANUAL TRIM panel
panels.text: This panel has the manual trim wheels for pitch, roll and yaw. Trim is a small adjustment so the plane flies straight without holding the stick.
panels.context: It is normally not needed because the plane trims itself in pitch and the pilot trims with the hat switch on the stick.

controls.name: ROLL TRIM wheel and indicator
controls.text: This wheel trims the plane in roll, so one wing does not drop. A scale shows how much trim is set.
controls.context: It is a backup for the trim switch on the stick.

controls.name: YAW TRIM knob
controls.text: This knob trims the plane in yaw, so the nose does not slide to one side. Dots show how much is set.
controls.context: Yaw trim corrects a sideways slide of the nose.

controls.name: PITCH TRIM wheel and indicator
controls.text: This wheel trims the plane in pitch, so the nose neither climbs nor sinks. A scale shows the setting.
controls.context: It is a backup for the trim switch on the stick.

controls.name: TRIM/AP DISC switch

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Pitch and roll trim from the stick switch or this panel. The autopilot is allowed.

positions.name: DISC
positions.text: Trim only from this panel. The stick trim switch and the autopilot are off.

controls.text: This switch decides where the trim commands come from. In DISC only this panel trims and the autopilot cannot be used.
controls.context: It is used if the trim switch on the stick fails.

panels.name: TEST panel
panels.text: This panel has test switches for system checks (BIT, built-in tests) and the test of all the cockpit lights.
panels.context: The pilot uses it during the start-up checks.

controls.name: FIRE & OHEAT DETECT test button
controls.text: Pressing this button tests the fire and overheat sensors. The ENG FIRE and OVERHEAT lights come on, and so does MASTER CAUTION.
controls.context: It shows that the fire warning system works. The training manual checks that the ENG FIRE light, the OVERHEAT caution light and MASTER CAUTION come on while the button is held.

controls.name: OBOGS BIT switch
controls.text: This switch starts a test of the onboard oxygen generator. The OXY LOW light stays on for 10 seconds and then goes out if all is well.
controls.context: OBOGS is a machine that makes breathing oxygen from engine air.

controls.name: MAL & IND LTS test button
controls.text: Pressing this button turns on all warning, caution and indicator lights and plays the voice messages.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to see that no bulb is dead.

controls.name: PROBE HEAT switch

positions.name: PROBE HEAT
positions.text: Heats the probes on the ground.

positions.name: TEST
positions.text: Tests the heater monitor. The PROBE HEAT caution flashes if ok.

controls.text: This switch heats the small tubes outside that measure speed and angle, so they do not freeze, when on the ground. It also tests the heater monitor.
controls.context: In flight the heat is always on.

controls.name: EPU/GEN test switch

positions.name: EPU/GEN
positions.text: Starts the test; it springs back.

controls.text: This switch tests the emergency generator on the ground without using the special fuel.
controls.context: It checks the power for the flight controls.

controls.name: FLCS PWR lights A-D
controls.text: Four lights A, B, C and D, one for each flight control channel. They show power to each during the test.
controls.context: Each light shows one channel is powered.

controls.name: FLCS PWR TEST switch

positions.name: MAINT
positions.text: For maintenance tests by ground crew.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Normal. Also used to test the EPU generator.

positions.name: TEST
positions.text: Tests the power to the channels.

controls.text: This switch tests the power to the flight control channels. It springs back from TEST to NORM.
controls.context: The MAINT position is meant for the ground crew.

areas.name: Right console
areas.text: The right console beside the pilot holds the sensor and avionics power switches, the HUD settings, the cockpit lights and air, the oxygen controls, the anti-ice and antenna switches, and a few small safety switches. The side stick sits on its front end.

panels.name: SNSR PWR control panel (sensor power)
panels.text: Four switches that give power to the plane's main sensors: the two pods under the air intake, the radar and the radar altimeter.
panels.context: The pilot switches them on during start-up when the aircraft is ready.

controls.name: LEFT HDPT switch
controls.text: This switch powers the pod on the left chin station, next to the engine air intake. It can be a pod such as the LANTIRN navigation pod or the HARM targeting pod.
controls.context: A station is a place under the plane where gear is hung. Pods need time to warm up, so they are powered on the ground.

controls.name: RIGHT HDPT switch
controls.text: This switch powers the pod on the right chin station, normally the targeting pod, a camera with zoom and laser.
controls.context: The pilot needs it to use the targeting pod. The camera of the pod needs several minutes to cool down, so it is switched on early.

controls.name: FCR switch (fire control radar)
controls.text: This switch gives power to the plane's radar (the fire control radar), which finds other aircraft and the ground. After power-up the radar runs a self-test of about three minutes.
controls.context: The radar must be on to track targets. It is also controlled by the RF switch.

controls.name: RDR ALT switch (radar altimeter)
controls.text: This switch controls the radar altimeter, which measures the height above the ground with a radar beam.
controls.context: STBY powers it without sending.

panels.name: HUD control panel
panels.text: Eight switches that decide what the HUD shows: scales, marks, brightness and test. The HUD is the glass in front of the pilot.
panels.context: The pilot sets them to remove clutter or to show what is needed for the current task.

controls.name: HUD Scales switch

positions.name: VV/VAH
positions.text: Vertical velocity, speed, altitude and heading scales.

positions.name: VAH
positions.text: Speed, altitude and heading scales only.

controls.text: This switch decides which scales the HUD draws for speed, height, climb rate and heading.
controls.context: The scales can be removed to leave only numbers.

controls.name: HUD Flightpath Marker switch

positions.name: ATT/FPM
positions.text: Pitch ladder (attitude bars), flight path marker and steering cue.

positions.name: FPM
positions.text: Flight path marker and steering cue only.

controls.text: This switch decides if the HUD shows the pitch ladder and the flight path marker, the mark that shows where the plane is really going.
controls.context: The marker shows the true path in wind.

controls.name: HUD DED/PFLD data switch

positions.name: DED DATA
positions.text: The DED data are repeated at the bottom of the HUD.

positions.name: PFL
positions.text: The pilot fault list is repeated at the bottom of the HUD.

controls.text: This switch copies the small text screen (DED) or the fault list (PFLD) to the bottom of the HUD.
controls.context: The pilot can read data without looking down.

controls.name: HUD Depressible Reticle switch
controls.text: This switch turns on the manual bombing circle on the HUD.
controls.context: The circle is moved with the RET DEPR knob on the keypad.

controls.name: HUD Velocity switch
controls.text: This switch decides which kind of speed the HUD shows: indicated, true or over the ground.
controls.context: The HUD goes back to indicated speed when the gear is down.

controls.name: HUD Altitude switch

positions.name: RADAR
positions.text: The scale shows radar altitude, the height above the ground.

positions.name: BARO
positions.text: The scale shows barometric altitude, the height above sea level.

positions.name: AUTO
positions.text: Barometric above 1500 feet, radar below that.

controls.text: This switch decides which height the HUD shows on its altitude scale: radar height, air-pressure height, or automatic.
controls.context: In AUTO the HUD shows air-pressure height above 1500 feet and radar height below that.

controls.name: HUD Brightness control switch

positions.name: AUTO BRT
positions.text: The HUD sets its brightness by itself.

controls.text: This switch chooses how the brightness of the HUD is set: day, night or automatic.
controls.context: The knob on the keypad fine tunes it.

controls.name: HUD TEST switch
controls.text: This switch would test the HUD. The BMS manual says it is not implemented.
controls.context: It is meant to check the display.

panels.name: Interior LIGHTING control panel
panels.text: This panel has the knobs that set the brightness of the cockpit lights, panel backlights and flood lights. Most cockpit lighting is green for night vision goggles.
panels.context: The pilot uses these knobs at night.

controls.name: PRIMARY CONSOLES knob
controls.text: This knob sets the backlight of the panels on the left aux console, left console and right console.
controls.context: A backlight lights the printed labels from behind.

controls.name: PRIMARY INST PNL knob
controls.text: This knob sets the backlight of the instrument panel and right aux console.
controls.context: It is the night light of the instruments.

controls.name: PRIMARY DATA ENTRY DISPLAY knob
controls.text: This knob sets the brightness of the small text screen (DED) and the fault list display.
controls.context: The pilot dims them at night so they do not dazzle.

controls.name: FLOOD CONSOLES knob
controls.text: This knob sets the flood lights on the consoles, lamps that light a whole area.
controls.context: It helps to read the console in the dark.

controls.name: FLOOD INST PNL knob
controls.text: This knob sets the flood lights on the instrument panel and right aux console.
controls.context: It helps to read the instruments.

controls.name: MAL & IND LTS switch
controls.text: This switch sets the brightness of the warning and indicator lights and the decoy counters to bright or dim.
controls.context: Bright is used automatically if the panel dimmer is fully off.

panels.name: AIR COND control panel
panels.text: This panel controls the cockpit air: temperature and the source of fresh air.
panels.context: Cockpit air is also needed for pressure and cooling of electronics.

controls.name: TEMP knob
controls.text: This knob is for the cockpit temperature. The BMS manuals do not describe what it does.
controls.context: Air conditioning keeps the pilot comfortable and cools the electronics.

controls.name: AIR SOURCE knob

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Closes the engine air valves. Cooling and pressure stop.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: Automatic control of temperature and pressure.

controls.text: This knob chooses where cockpit air comes from. OFF stops cooling and pressure and the fuel transfer from drop tanks. The manual marks DUMP and RAM as not implemented in BMS.
controls.context: NORM is the normal setting and must be used on the ramp, or the EQUIP HOT light comes on and the avionics get too hot.

panels.name: OXYGEN regulator panel
panels.text: This panel controls the breathing oxygen to the pilot's mask. BMS models the oxygen system only in part.
panels.context: High up the air is too thin to breathe, so the pilot gets oxygen. In BMS the pilot suffers lack of oxygen if the oxygen supply is not turned on.

controls.name: OXYGEN FLOW indicator
controls.text: A small window that blinks white and black. White means oxygen flows.
controls.context: A glance shows if the mask is getting oxygen. The BMS manual gives no further details of this indicator.

controls.name: OXYGEN SUPPLY pressure indicator
controls.text: A gauge for the oxygen pressure. The real aircraft's normal range is 10 to 55 psi.
controls.context: A low value means a problem with the supply. The BMS manual gives no further details of this gauge.

controls.name: EMERGENCY lever

positions.name: TEST MASK
positions.text: Maximum oxygen under pressure; for leak tests by ground crew.

controls.text: This lever sets the pressure breathing mode. The BMS training manual says only the green SUPPLY lever is implemented, so this lever has no effect.
controls.context: In the real aircraft EMERGENCY gives full oxygen under pressure and TEST MASK is for the life support crew.

controls.name: Diluter lever

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: A mix of air and oxygen (no effect in BMS).

controls.text: This lever chooses pure oxygen or a mix of oxygen and cockpit air. In BMS it has no effect, as only the green SUPPLY lever is implemented.
controls.context: In the real aircraft NORM mixes air and oxygen depending on the cabin altitude.

controls.name: SUPPLY lever (oxygen supply)

positions.name: PBG
positions.text: Oxygen on, with pressure breathing in hard turns.

controls.text: This lever switches the oxygen to the mask on or off. PBG also adds pressure breathing in hard turns to help the pilot stay awake. In BMS it is the one oxygen lever that works.
controls.context: Switched on, it supplies the mask (and starts the breathing sounds) and keeps the pilot from lack of oxygen at high cabin altitude. The pilot sets it before flight.

panels.name: ANTI ICE and ANT SEL switches
panels.text: Three switches: one for engine ice protection and two for choosing the antennas of the IFF and the UHF radio.
panels.context: Antennas sit above and below the plane. The pilot can choose one if the other is shadowed.

controls.name: ENGINE ANTI-ICE switch

positions.name: AUTO
positions.text: The heaters turn on by themselves if ice is found.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The heaters and the ice detector are off.

controls.text: This switch controls the heaters that stop ice in the engine intake.
controls.context: AUTO turns them on when ice is sensed.

controls.name: IFF ANT SEL switch
controls.text: This switch would choose the antenna that the IFF uses. The BMS manual says the ANT SEL switches are not implemented; IFF works equally in all directions.
controls.context: In the real aircraft antennas sit above and below the plane.

controls.name: UHF ANT SEL switch
controls.text: This switch would choose the antenna of the UHF radio. The BMS manual says the ANT SEL switches are not implemented; the radio works equally in all directions.
controls.context: In the real aircraft the radio switches between the upper and lower antenna in NORM.

panels.name: AVIONICS POWER control panel
panels.text: This panel switches on the electronic systems one by one and has the knob for the plane's navigation system (INS).
panels.context: At start-up, the pilot turns them on in order after the engine runs. The INS needs a few minutes to align.

controls.name: MMC switch (mission computer)
controls.text: This switch gives power to the main computer of the plane, the modular mission computer.
controls.context: Many avionics systems depend on the main computer.

controls.name: ST STA switch (stores stations)
controls.text: Powers the places under the wings where weapons and tanks are hung.
controls.context: Weapons on the stations need this power.

controls.name: MFD switch
controls.text: This switch gives power to both multi-function screens (MFDs). The screens need a few seconds to start up.
controls.context: The screens stay dark without it.

controls.name: UFC switch
controls.text: This switch gives power to the keypad (ICP) and the small text screen (DED). They need a few seconds to start up.
controls.context: Without it no data can be typed on the keypad.

controls.name: MAP switch
controls.text: A switch for a map system. The BMS manual says the MAP switch is not functional.
controls.context: Nothing in the cockpit depends on it.

controls.name: GPS switch
controls.text: Powers the GPS receiver, which uses satellites to find the position. The BMS manual says aircraft with the embedded GPS/INS (EGI) no longer have this switch; it belongs to the older panel.
controls.context: On those aircraft the GPS comes with the navigation system.

controls.name: DL switch (datalink)
controls.text: This switch gives power to the datalink, which shares positions by radio.
controls.context: Datalink shares positions of friends and targets between aircraft.

controls.name: INS knob (navigation system)

positions.name: ALIGN NORM
positions.text: The normal alignment on the ground.

positions.name: NAV
positions.text: Normal navigation after the alignment is finished.

positions.name: CAL
positions.text: The manual does not describe this position.

positions.name: IN FLT ALIGN
positions.text: Alignment in the air, with the help of the GPS.

controls.text: This knob switches on the inertial navigation system (INS, with GPS) and chooses how it aligns. The INS always knows where the plane is. The plane must not move while it aligns.
controls.context: With the embedded GPS/INS a full alignment takes about four minutes. Navigation marks show only after the knob is set to NAV. The manual says ALIGN STOR HDG and ATT are not implemented.

controls.name: MIDS LVT knob (TACAN and datalink)

positions.name: ZERO
positions.text: Erases the data of the terminal.

controls.text: This knob powers the MIDS terminal, which provides the TACAN radio beacon receiver and the Link 16 datalink with other aircraft. ZERO erases the secret data in the terminal.
controls.context: Without power for this terminal the TACAN shows as off.

panels.name: Right console switches
panels.text: Small switches on the right console: voice messages, data erasing, the seat height and the coded radio.
panels.context: The pilot rarely touches these switches.

controls.name: PLAIN / CIPHER switch
controls.text: This switch chooses clear or coded radio. The BMS manual says the PLAIN/CIPHER switch is not implemented.
controls.context: Coded means the voice is scrambled so it stays secret.

controls.name: VOICE MESSAGE switch
controls.text: This switch silences the voice messages of the plane when set to INHIBIT.
controls.context: It is used only when a message repeats wrongly. In normal flight the switch stays at VOICE MESSAGE.

controls.name: ZEROIZE switch
controls.text: This switch is meant to erase secret data from the plane's systems in an emergency. The BMS manual says the Zeroize switch is not implemented.
controls.context: It is used if the plane might fall into enemy hands.

controls.name: SEAT ADJ switch
controls.text: This switch raises or lowers the seat with a motor. It must be held and springs back to the middle.
controls.context: The pilot sets the seat for a comfortable view through the HUD.

controls.name: NUCLEAR CONSENT switch
controls.text: This switch is part of the nuclear weapon system. It is not implemented and has no consequence in BMS.
controls.context: The training manual calls the nuclear circuit irrelevant in BMS.

panels.name: KY-58 secure voice panel
panels.text: The control box of the KY-58, a coded voice unit that scrambles radio talk. The BMS manual says it is not implemented.
panels.context: It would be used for secure radio talk.

controls.name: KY-58 secure voice panel
controls.text: The control box of the coded voice unit with its knobs for volume, mode, power and code. The BMS manual says the KY-58 is not implemented.
controls.context: Coded voice is not used in BMS.

areas.name: Ejection seat
areas.text: The ejection seat is the seat that shoots the pilot out of the plane in an emergency. Its handles are on and under the seat.

panels.name: Ejection seat controls
panels.text: The handles of the ejection seat: the arming lever, the ejection handle and the manual parachute lever.
panels.context: The seat must be armed in flight and made safe on the ground.

controls.name: Ejection seat arming lever

positions.name: ARMED
positions.text: Folded down, flush with the seat. The seat is armed and the handle works.

positions.name: SAFE
positions.text: Upright. The seat is safe and the SEAT NOT ARMED caution is lit.

controls.text: This lever arms the seat so the ejection handle works. Upright it is safe, and the SEAT NOT ARMED caution light is on. Folded down it is armed.
controls.context: The pilot arms the seat before taxiing; the ground crew makes it safe on the ground.

controls.name: Ejection handle
controls.text: Pulling this handle (PULL TO EJECT) ejects the pilot. The canopy is thrown off first and then the seat is fired by a rocket.
controls.context: The seat picks the right way to open the parachute by itself, depending on speed and height.

controls.name: EMERGENCY MANUAL CHUTE lever
controls.text: Pulling this lever about six inches opens the parachute by hand and frees the pilot from the seat, if this does not happen by itself.
controls.context: It is a backup after an ejection.

areas.name: Stick and throttle
areas.text: The pilot's hands rest on the side stick (right hand) and the throttle (left hand). Many switches on them are used without letting go of the controls (HOTAS: hands on throttle and stick).

panels.name: Side stick controller
panels.text: A short stick on the right console that senses force and barely moves. The flight computers read the push and send commands to the control surfaces. It also carries many buttons for the thumb and fingers.
panels.context: Pushing or pulling the stick pitches the nose. Moving it sideways rolls the plane. The buttons on its head are used without letting go of the stick (HOTAS: hands on throttle and stick).

controls.name: Weapon release button (WPN REL)
controls.text: Pressing this red button on the top left of the stick head fires an air-to-air missile or releases a bomb or another weapon at the ground. For the AMRAAM missile the button is held for about one second.
controls.context: The MASTER ARM switch has to be set first. In the selective jettison mode the same button drops the chosen stores, and in the DTOS mode it marks the target.

controls.name: Trim button (4-way)
controls.text: This four-way button on top of the grip trims the plane: forward for nose down, aft for nose up, left for the left wing down and right for the right wing down. Trim is a small adjustment so the plane flies straight without holding force on the stick.
controls.context: Stick trim does not work while the autopilot is engaged; the manual trim wheels on the left console still do.

controls.name: Trigger (two-stage)
controls.text: The trigger has two stops. In the air-to-ground modes the first stop fires the laser of the targeting pod (the laser measures distance and guides bombs). Squeezed to the second stop it fires the gun.
controls.context: The LASER ARM switch on the MISC panel must be at LASER ARM before the laser can fire.

controls.name: NWS / A/R DISC / MSL STEP button
controls.text: This button on the front of the grip, below the trigger, has several jobs. On the ground it switches nosewheel steering on and off. In flight with the refuelling door open it disconnects the tanker's boom. In the air-to-air modes it steps to the next missile station, and a press of about half a second picks the next missile type.
controls.context: In the air-to-ground modes it steps through the bomb delivery modes (CCRP, CCIP, DTOS) or to the next missile of the AGM-65, IAM or HARM type.

controls.name: Target Management Switch (TMS)
controls.text: A four-way switch at the top right of the stick head, moved with the thumb. Forward picks, designates or locks a target. Aft drops the target again or rejects it. Left and right do other jobs that depend on the sensor, for example IFF questions to a target or switching the radar between its search modes.
controls.context: What happens depends on the sensor of interest (SOI): the radar, the targeting pod, the HUD or a missile display. The HOTAS table lists every direction for every mode.

controls.name: Display Management Switch (DMS)
controls.text: A four-way switch at the left side of the stick head. Forward makes the HUD the active display (the sensor of interest). Aft hands that role to the screens (MFDs) and swaps between them. Left and right change the page of the left and right screen. Aft held for half a second turns the helmet display marks on or off.
controls.context: It lets the pilot change screens and pages without touching them and without taking the hand off the stick.

controls.name: Countermeasures Management Switch (CMS)
controls.text: A four-way switch at the lower right of the stick head for the chaff and flare dispenser and the jammer. Forward fires the manual program chosen on the CMDS panel (1 to 4). Aft gives consent to the dispenser or the jammer. Left fires program 6. Right stops the jammer and takes the consent back.
controls.context: How it reacts depends on the MODE knob of the CMDS panel. On the F-16I Sufa the jammer system is IDIAS: there, left steps it through standby, avionics and jammer, and right puts it back to standby.

controls.name: Expand / FOV button
controls.text: A button on the lower rear of the grip, pressed with the little finger. It changes the picture of the active sensor between a normal and a zoomed (expanded) view, for example for the radar, the map or the targeting pod.
controls.context: With the missile screens it changes the field of view of the seeker; with the HARM missile it chooses the position mode.

controls.name: Paddle switch
controls.text: A lever on the lower front of the grip, pulled with the little finger. While it is held, the autopilot is switched off so the pilot can steer by hand. It can also interrupt a fly-up of the terrain-following radar.
controls.context: When the lever is let go, the autopilot takes the new position as its reference. It is used together with the autopilot switches on the MISC panel.

controls.name: Side stick controller (pitch and roll)
controls.text: The short stick on the right console. It barely moves, about a quarter of an inch; the flight control computers read how hard the pilot pushes. Pushing forward points the nose down, pulling points it up, and pushing sideways rolls the plane.
controls.context: The computers turn the force into commands for the control surfaces, which is why the stick feels so stiff.

panels.name: Throttle
panels.text: The throttle lever above the left console. It sets the engine power and carries the switches for radio, radar, speed brakes and the fighting modes. It has stops at OFF, IDLE, MIL and MAX AB.
panels.context: Forward of MIL the afterburner starts. OFF stops the engine. The switches on the grip are used without letting go of the throttle.

controls.name: COMM switch (radio transmit)
controls.text: A four-way switch at the top front of the throttle grip. Forward transmits on the VHF radio (COM 2), aft on the UHF radio (COM 1). Left and right send or clear datalink information, such as the radar cursor position or the selected steerpoint.
controls.context: It is the push-to-talk button of the plane. The keypad display highlights the radio that is keyed.

controls.name: MAN RNG / UNCAGE knob
controls.text: A knob on top of the throttle grip that can be turned and pushed. Turning it changes the gain of the radar ground map or the zoom of the targeting pod. A short push uncages the seeker of the AIM-9 missile or declutters the HUD. In the air-to-ground mode a long push selects the gun for strafing.
controls.context: What it does depends on the master mode and on the sensor that is active.

controls.name: DOGFIGHT / MISSILE OVERRIDE switch
controls.text: This three-position slide switch on the outer front of the throttle grip overrides the master mode. Out gives the dogfight mode, in gives the missile override mode, and the middle goes back to the earlier mode.
controls.context: It gets the plane ready for a close air fight in one move, with the radar and weapons set as saved before the flight.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: Dogfight mode: radar ready for close combat, gun and missiles available.

positions.name: CENTER
positions.text: Back to the previous mode: air-to-air, air-to-ground or navigation.

positions.name: IN
positions.text: Missile override mode: the radar and the missile are set up for a quick shot.

controls.name: SPD BRK switch (speed brakes)
controls.text: A slide switch on the inner side of the throttle grip, moved with the thumb. Aft opens the speed brakes, the middle stops them where they are and forward closes them. The aft position springs back to the middle.
controls.context: Speed brakes are panels that open into the wind to slow the plane down. The pilot leaves the switch forward to avoid creeping.

positions.name: AFT
positions.text: Opens the speed brakes; the switch springs back to the middle.

positions.name: CENTER
positions.text: The speed brakes stay where they are.

controls.name: RDR CURSOR / ENABLE (ministick)
controls.text: A small force-sensing stick for the thumb on the inner side of the grip. Pushing it moves the cursor on the screens, on the HUD or on the targeting pod, and in close combat it moves the radar antenna. Pressing it down enables functions. Up and down bump the radar range, left and right the width of the radar scan.
controls.context: It is the mouse of the cockpit. The sensor that is active decides what the cursor moves.

controls.name: Cutoff release
controls.text: A small lever under the throttle grip. Pressing it lets the throttle go from IDLE down to OFF, which stops the engine.
controls.context: It stops the engine being shut off by accident. The throttle also has to be turned outward to pass the OFF stop.

controls.name: ANT ELEV knob (radar antenna tilt)
controls.text: A thumbwheel on the front of the throttle grip with a click in the middle. Rolling it up tilts the radar antenna up, rolling it down tilts it down, and the middle position levels it again.
controls.context: It decides where the radar looks. It does not work in the close-combat and some tracking modes.

controls.name: Throttle (engine power lever)
controls.text: The lever itself, above the left console, with stops at OFF, IDLE, MIL and MAX AB. Pushing it forward gives more power. Beyond MIL the afterburner starts.
controls.context: Moving it from OFF to IDLE gives the engine fuel and ignition for the start. The throttle must be turned outward to pass the stop between MIL and the afterburner.
